title: Latency-horizon admission gate & kernel-fit arbiter for continuous batching
creator: Lara Chen
description: Background: Continuous batching at scale occasionally yields multi-modal tail behavior driven by mismatches between admission decisions, kernel selection latency, and attention prefetch timing. Goal: Implement a lightweight admission gate that reasons over a short 'latency horizon' (next 50-200ms) to accept/hold requests, plus a kernel-fit arbiter that chooses the most appropriate kernel variant (quantized, grouped-attention, or fallback) at admission time. The combined system should smooth microbursts, reduce 95th/99th percentile token latency, and avoid throughput regressions. Approach: 1) Add an admission horizon buffer that tracks incoming request size, sequence-length distribution, and current KV-cache pressure. 2) Compute a small lookahead cost model to decide accept/hold/route-to-degraded-path. 3) At admission, consult a kernel-fit arbiter that maps request shape + hardware signals to a preferred kernel and pre-schedules attention prefetch/prefill work. 4) Provide observability hooks (decision reasons, predicted vs actual latency) and a canary rollout plan. Constraints: must be incremental (config flags), low CPU overhead, and compatible with Dedicated capacity isolation and Private deployments. Success metrics are defined below.
acceptance_criteria: 95th-percentile per-token latency reduced by >= 20% for mixed short/long workloads in our synthetic microburst suite
99th-percentile per-token latency reduced by >= 15% without reducing median throughput by more than 5%
No increased OOMs or KV-cache evictions in Dedicated runs compared to baseline
Observable decision logs (admit/hold/route) available in Console with per-key metrics
Canary rollout with automated rollback triggers based on latency and error-rate thresholds
progress_updates: 2026-03-01: Scoping and hypothesis doc drafted. Benchmarked baseline microburst behavior on runtime-1.20; observed bimodal tail at 95/99 percentiles for mixed-llm traffic.
2026-03-04: Small cost model prototype implemented (lua rule + lightweight estimator). Initial offline sims show 18% reduction in 95p latency for short-heavy bursts when holding 30-50ms.

2026-03-06: Design review with ML infra and kernel team. Decided to implement kernel-fit arbiter as a pluggable policy that can prefer grouped-attention kernels for long-seq requests and quantized kernels for short-seq high-concurrency requests.

2026-03-08: Trade-off discussion: aggressive hold reduces tail but increases median latency for interactive short requests. We agreed on latency-horizon backoff schedule and tenant-aware thresholds for Dedicated customers.

2026-03-10: Started instrumentation work and added observability schema. Created feature flag and canary config. Implementation of arbiter scheduling hooks underway (PR branch: feat/eng/ENG-337521-kernel-arbiter).
2026-03-10: Noted action item: add unit tests for decision logic and integrate with existing admission metrics pipeline (ENG-531210).
qa_notes: Test plan: run synthetic microburst suite (short/long mix, 5-40 concurrent streams) against staging runtime-1.21 with feature flag enabled and compare median/95/99 token latency to baseline
Canary: start with 2% of production traffic on hosted API, monitor per-tenant thresholds and abort if 95p token latency regresses by >10% or error-rate increases >0.1%
Failure modes: over-holding leading to request queuing spikes; incorrect kernel selection causing slowdowns for long sequences. Add kill-switch and fallback to baseline kernel path.
